note.text:
Volume is the space a body takes up. Its SI unit is the cubic metre (m³). We also use cm³, litres (L) and millilitres (mL): 1 L = 1000 mL = 1000 cm³, so 1 mL = 1 cm³; 1 m³ = 1000 L.
• Liquids: pour into a measuring cylinder; put your eye level with the surface and read at the bottom of the curved surface (the meniscus).
• Regular solids: volume of a cuboid = length × width × height.
• Irregular solids (a stone): put water in a measuring cylinder and read it; lower the stone in and read again. Volume of the stone = second reading − first reading (displacement).

worked_example.problem: Ewane puts water in a measuring cylinder, then lowers a stone into it. What is the volume of the stone?
steps: Before: the bottom of the meniscus is at {a} mL.
Volume of the stone = {b} − {a} = {b - a} mL = {b - a} cm³.

cards.idea: Volume is the space a body takes up. 1 L = {factor('L', 'mL')} mL = {factor('L', 'cm³')} cm³, so 1 mL = 1 cm³.
example: A {v} mL bottle of water holds {convertUnit(v, 'mL', 'cm³')} cm³ of water.

cards.idea: Read a measuring cylinder with your eye level with the surface, at the bottom of the curve (the meniscus).
example: The bottom of the meniscus is on {v} mL.

cards.idea: A cuboid: volume = length × width × height.
example: A box {l} cm × {w} cm × {h} cm: {l} × {w} × {h} = {cuboid(l, w, h)} cm³.

cards.idea: An irregular solid: read the water level before and after the stone goes in. The difference is the stone's volume.
example: Before {a} mL, after {b} mL: the stone is {b - a} cm³.

questions.prompt: How much water is in the measuring cylinder?

misconceptions.explain: Read at the bottom of the curved surface, not at the edges.

questions.hint: Each small mark is {step} mL. Look at the bottom of the curve.
solution: The bottom of the meniscus is on {answer} mL.

questions.prompt: A {it} is {l} cm long, {w} cm wide and {h} cm high. What is its volume?

misconceptions.explain: Volume = length × width × height: multiply, do not add.

questions.prompt: What is the volume of the stone, in cm³?

misconceptions.explain: That is the water and the stone together. Subtract the reading before the stone went in.

solution: Before: {2 * a} mL. After: {2 * a + 2 * d} mL.
Stone = {2 * a + 2 * d} − {2 * a} = {answer} mL = {answer} cm³.

questions.prompt: A water tank is {l} m long, {w} m wide and {h} m high. How many litres of water can it hold?

misconceptions.explain: That is in cubic metres. 1 m³ = 1000 L.

solution: 1 m³ = {factor('m³', 'L')} L, so the tank holds {answer} L.

questions.prompt: Convert this volume: {up ? k / 10 : k * 10} {up ? p.a : p.b} = ? {up ? p.b : p.a}
questions.answer: up ? convertUnit(k / 10, p.a, p.b) : convertUnit(k * 10, p.b, p.a)

misconceptions.wrong: up ? convertUnit(k / 10, p.b, p.a) : convertUnit(k * 10, p.a, p.b)
misconceptions.explain: You went the wrong way. From a bigger unit to a smaller one, the number gets bigger; from smaller to bigger, it gets smaller.

solution: {up ? 'Multiply' : 'Divide'} by {factor(p.a, p.b)}: {up ? k / 10 : k * 10} {up ? p.a : p.b} = {answer} {up ? p.b : p.a}.

questions.where: d + e + f != d * e * f
questions.prompt: One answer is wrong. Which one?

right.text: A box {a} cm × {b} cm × {c} cm has a volume of {a * b * c} cm³.
right.truth: cuboid(a, b, c) == a * b * c

right.text: Water rises from {2 * x} mL to {2 * x + 2 * y} mL: the stone is {2 * y} cm³.

wrong.text: A box {d} cm × {e} cm × {f} cm has a volume of {d + e + f} cm³.
wrong.truth: d + e + f == cuboid(d, e, f)
wrong.explain: Multiply, do not add: {d} × {e} × {f} = {cuboid(d, e, f)} cm³.
